CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Go into the G20 Trump-Xi dinner seeking a truce that freezes tariffs at current levels and defers the Jan 1, 2019 jump of List 3 from 10% to 25%, rather than escalating further or making unilateral purchase concessions. Position ourselves as the defender of the multilateral trading order while holding firm on core red lines (no capitulation on industrial policy). Use the meeting to lock in a negotiating framework that pauses the escalation schedule, buying time before the worst of the tariff hit lands in Q1 2019.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat is high but not existential — approximately +0.45. The US has imposed Section 301 tariffs on roughly $250B of our exports (Lists 1 and 2 at 25%, List 3 at 10% per the Sept 24 entry), and List 3 is scheduled to rise to 25% on Jan 1, 2019, with Trump threatening to cover the remaining ~$500B+ of exports if unresolved. The domestic cost is material: China's official manufacturing PMI fell to 50.2 in October — the lowest in over two years and barely above the contraction line — with new export orders contracting a fifth straight month to 46.9 (a 34-month low), reflecting the tariffs' bite after the $200B List 3 took effect in late September. FX pressure is visible in the yuan's depreciation to ~6.95, near the psychologically important 7.0 level (DEXCHUS series). Firm-level targeting is already real (ZTE denial order April 16) and Huawei is an open risk. This is tempered by genuine headroom: ample reserves, scope for stimulus, and exports that still grew ~11% y/y in October on front-loading. The action stance is de-escalatory at the margin (+0.15, negotiate): escalating further would risk tariffing the entire export base and a full-blown trade war that analysts estimate could shave over 1pp off 2019 GDP growth, while the G20 moment and Trump's own signals of wanting a deal and his market anxiety (October VIX spiked to ~25) give us a narrow window to secure a ceasefire before the Jan 1 escalation. We should not yet make purchase concessions — no matching offer has been made and talks are not sufficiently advanced — so negotiate, not concede.
key_factors: US Section 301 tariffs cover ~$250B of Chinese exports (Lists 1&2 at 25%, List 3 at 10%, rising to 25% on Jan 1 2019)
China manufacturing PMI 50.2 in Oct (2-yr low); export orders contracting 5 straight months (46.9)
Yuan depreciated to ~6.95 near the 7.0 psychological level
ZTE denial order; Huawei firm-level targeting risk
Trump-Xi G20 meeting imminent (Nov 1 call established agenda); Trump signaling willingness to deal amid US market volatility
China has stimulus headroom and reserves; exports up ~11% y/y in Oct on front-loading

sources_cited.excerpt: List 3 takes effect at 10%. China imposes retaliatory tariffs (5-10%) on ~$60B of US goods. Combined US Section 301 coverage now ~$250B of Chinese imports.
Trump directs USTR to finalize List 3: 10% tariffs on ~$200B of Chinese imports effective Sept 24, scheduled to rise to 25% on Jan 1, 2019.
US Commerce Department bans ZTE from buying US components (denial order).
Trump and Xi hold a phone call focused on trade; agree to meet at the G20 in Argentina.
Yuan depreciated from ~6.81 in Aug to ~6.95 by Nov 28, 2018, approaching the 7.0 level.
China's manufacturing PMI fell to 50.2 in October (lowest in 2+ years); new export orders contracted a 5th straight month to 46.9; non-manufacturing dropped to 53.9.
China's October exports up ~11% y/y (front-loading); GDP growth weakest in nearly a decade in Q3 2018.
Trump projecting tough talk but signaling willingness to make a deal with Xi at the G20; West Wing divided between hawks (Navarro/Lighthizer) and doves (Mnuchin/Kudlow).
